subject: Chemistry
description: Metallurgy — extraction of metals (iron, aluminium, copper), reactivity series, electrolytic refining, alloys, blast furnace.

questions.stem: ALUMINIUM is extracted from BAUXITE ore by:
questions.explanation: ALUMINIUM EXTRACTION — Hall-Héroult Process (1886, independently invented by Charles Hall in USA + Paul Héroult in France). STEPS: (1) BAUXITE (Al₂O₃·xH₂O) is purified to ALUMINA (Al₂O₃) via BAYER PROCESS (treat with NaOH, dissolve as Na[Al(OH)₄], precipitate as Al(OH)₃, calcine to Al₂O₃). (2) ALUMINA is dissolved in MOLTEN CRYOLITE (Na₃AlF₆) — lowers melting point from ~2050°C to ~960°C. (3) ELECTROLYSIS in CARBON-LINED steel cell: cathode = molten Al collects at bottom; anode = carbon blocks consumed (oxidized to CO₂). REACTIONS: at cathode Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; at anode 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (then C + O₂ → CO₂). HUGE ELECTRICITY needed: ~13-15 kWh per kg of Al. INDIA: aluminium plants located NEAR HYDROELECTRIC plants (cheap power) — Hirakud (Odisha-NALCO), Korba (Chhattisgarh-BALCO), Renukoot (UP-HINDALCO). MAJOR INDIAN PRODUCERS: Vedanta, HINDALCO, NALCO, BALCO. USES OF Al: (1) Aircraft, automobile bodies (light + corrosion-resistant). (2) Electrical cables (cheaper than copper, less density). (3) Cookware, foil. (4) Doors, windows, packaging. (5) Beverage cans. RECYCLING: Al is HIGHLY RECYCLABLE — only 5% of original energy needed for re-melting. PYQ FREQUENCY: Hall-Héroult in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: IRON is extracted from HEMATITE ore in a:
questions.explanation: IRON EXTRACTION — BLAST FURNACE process: HEMATITE (Fe₂O₃) + COKE (Carbon) + LIMESTONE (CaCO₃) added at top; HOT AIR blasted from bottom. KEY REACTIONS: (1) C + O₂ → CO₂ (combustion). (2) CO₂ + C → 2CO (CO is the actual reducer). (3) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (REDUCTION at top). (4) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (decomposes). (5) CaO + SiO₂ (silica impurity) → CaSiO₃ (SLAG, removes impurities; SLAG floats on molten iron, drained separately). PRODUCT: PIG IRON (~93% iron, 4% C, plus Si, Mn, P, S impurities) — collected at bottom. CONVERSION TO STEEL: pig iron processed in BASIC OXYGEN FURNACE (BOF) or ELECTRIC ARC FURNACE (EAF) — reduces carbon to ~0.1-2%. INDIAN STEEL: SAIL (Steel Authority of India), Tata Steel, JSW are major producers. KEY PLANTS: Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Bokaro (Jharkhand), Rourkela (Odisha) — built post-Independence with USSR, UK, Germany cooperation respectively. INDIA is 2ND LARGEST CRUDE STEEL PRODUCER (after China; ~135 million tonnes/yr 2024). UPSC angle: steel sector is core to industrial growth — covered in GS-3 (economy/infrastructure). KEY CHALLENGES: pollution (steel sector ~7-8% global CO₂ emissions), competition from China. PYQ FREQUENCY: blast furnace in NEET, NCERT, SSC chemistry 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which metal is the MOST REACTIVE in the metal reactivity series?
questions.explanation: REACTIVITY SERIES (memorize for SSC, NEET, JEE-Main): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt. POTASSIUM is the MOST reactive shown (above K is a few even more reactive like Cs, Rb, Fr — but K is what's typically referenced in school chemistry). MNEMONIC: 'PSC Mg Aluminium Zinc Iron Pb (Hydrogen) Cu Hg Ag Au Pt' or 'Please Send Cute Monkeys And Zebras In Lions' Pen Hesitating Cause Hippo's Stink Awfully Past'. KEY OBSERVATIONS: (1) MOST REACTIVE (K, Na) — react VIOLENTLY with water, even cold; produce H₂ + heat (sometimes igniting); stored in KEROSENE/oil. (2) MODERATELY REACTIVE (Mg, Al) — react with hot water/steam; oxide layer protects (Al passivates). (3) Mid (Zn, Fe) — react slowly with steam, dilute acids. (4) BELOW HYDROGEN (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt) — DO NOT react with dilute acids; only with concentrated oxidizing acids. (5) GOLD, PLATINUM — extremely inert (jewelry). DISPLACEMENT REACTION: more reactive metal displaces less reactive from its salt: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (Fe more reactive, displaces Cu). UPSC GS angle: rare-earth metals + critical minerals strategy (lithium, cobalt, copper imports) is a contemporary policy issue. PYQ FREQUENCY: reactivity series order in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

questions.explanation: BRASS — alloy of COPPER (~70%) + ZINC (~30%); proportions vary by use. PROPERTIES: golden-yellow color, more workable than pure copper, corrosion-resistant. USES: musical instruments (trumpets, trombones, saxophones — 'brass band'), screws, locks, plumbing fittings, decorative items, ammunition cartridges (brass casings), idols (especially in India — kanchi/madurai brass idols). KEY ALLOYS to memorize: (1) BRASS — Cu + Zn. (2) BRONZE — Cu + Sn (the 'Bronze Age', ~3000 BCE; tools, statues, bells). (3) STEEL — Fe + C (~0.1-2% C); MILD steel ~0.2%, HIGH-CARBON steel ~0.7-1%. (4) STAINLESS STEEL — Fe + Cr (10-30%) + Ni; rust-resistant. (5) DURALUMIN — Al + Cu + Mg + Mn; light + strong; aircraft. (6) GERMAN SILVER — Cu + Zn + Ni (no actual silver, despite name). (7) SOLDER — Pb + Sn (lead-tin); used for joining wires. (8) PEWTER — Sn + Sb + Cu; tableware. (9) MAGNALIUM — Al + Mg; light-weight aircraft parts. (10) AMALGAM — Hg + other metals (dental fillings, gold extraction). HISTORICAL: Brass cymbals popular in many percussion sets; bronze coinage in ancient Rome, Greece, Mauryan India. PYQ FREQUENCY: alloy compositions in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests memory of alloy compositions.

questions.stem: ELECTROLYTIC REFINING is used to PURIFY which metal?

options.option_text: Sodium (electrolysis of NaCl is for extraction)

questions.explanation: ELECTROLYTIC REFINING of COPPER (most common application): impure copper as ANODE; pure copper as CATHODE; electrolyte is dilute CuSO₄ solution. PROCESS: (1) Apply DC current. (2) Anode oxidation: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (impure copper dissolves). (3) Cathode reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (pure copper deposits on cathode). (4) IMPURITIES separate: noble metals (Ag, Au, Pt) form 'ANODE MUD' (settles below); reactive impurities (Zn, Fe) stay in solution. RESULT: 99.99%+ pure copper — needed for electrical wiring (impurities reduce conductivity). ECONOMIC: ANODE MUD is rich in precious metals — selling it offsets refining costs! KEY: this works for any metal more LESS noble than the impurities you want to leave behind. OTHER ELECTROLYTIC REFINING: Zinc, Nickel, Lead, Silver, Gold (gold from copper anode mud is further refined). EXTRACTION (different from refining): (a) Aluminium — Hall-Héroult (extraction from molten Al₂O₃ in cryolite). (b) Sodium, potassium, magnesium — extracted from molten chlorides via electrolysis (Castner-Kellner / Down's process). (c) Iron — blast furnace (no electrolysis). DIFFERENCE — EXTRACTION (from ore) vs REFINING (purification of crude metal). UPSC angle: electricity-intensive metallurgy concerns (energy security, Net-Zero pathway). PYQ FREQUENCY: electrolytic refining in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

questions.explanation: RUSTING — slow oxidation of iron in presence of OXYGEN + WATER (moisture in air). RESULT: HYDRATED IRON OXIDE (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) — flaky, reddish-brown, weakens metal. CHEMISTRY: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·3H₂O (simplified). FACTORS that ACCELERATE rusting: (1) HUMID AIR (high water vapour). (2) SALT WATER (sea air corrosion fastest — chlorides accelerate). (3) ACID RAIN (low pH). (4) SCRATCHED metal (exposes iron beneath any protective layer). PREVENTION methods: (1) PAINTING — barrier between iron and air/water. (2) GREASING/OILING — moving parts. (3) GALVANIZING — coating with zinc; zinc is more reactive, corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection). (4) CHROME PLATING — decorative + protective. (5) STAINLESS STEEL — alloy with Cr (>10.5%); chromium oxide layer protects. (6) BLUEING (gun metal) — controlled oxidation creating protective Fe₃O₄ layer. INDIA: ~$ billions lost annually to rust/corrosion (railway tracks, bridges, ships, infrastructure). KEY: dry oxygen alone DOES NOT rust iron quickly — needs MOISTURE. Boiled distilled water + iron in airless container also doesn't rust. EXPERIMENT: 3 test tubes — (a) iron + distilled water, no air → no rust. (b) iron + dry air → no rust. (c) iron + air + water → rust. UPSC angle: corrosion engineering, infrastructure life-cycle costs. PYQ FREQUENCY: rusting in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which method is used to extract HIGHLY REACTIVE metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al)?
questions.explanation: EXTRACTION method depends on REACTIVITY of the metal: (1) HIGHLY REACTIVE METALS (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) — at top of reactivity series; their oxides are TOO STABLE to be reduced by ordinary reducers (C, CO). EXTRACT via ELECTROLYSIS of MOLTEN SALTS (chlorides, hydroxides, oxides). Examples: NaCl(molten) — sodium at cathode (Castner-Kellner / Down's process); MgCl₂(molten) — Mg at cathode; Al₂O₃ in cryolite — Hall-Héroult. (2) MODERATELY REACTIVE (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) — REDUCED with CARBON (coke) in BLAST FURNACE or similar. (3) LEAST REACTIVE (Ag, Au, Pt) — found NATIVE (uncombined) in nature; mined directly + purified. KEY: discovery of HIGHLY REACTIVE metals was DELAYED until ELECTRICITY was harnessed (early 1800s): (a) HUMPHRY DAVY (UK, 1807) — discovered POTASSIUM, SODIUM via electrolysis of molten potash, soda. (b) Davy also discovered Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba (1808). EARLIER metals (Cu, Au, Ag, Pb, Sn) — known since antiquity (Bronze Age). HALL-HÉROULT (1886) for Al — before this, Al was MORE EXPENSIVE than gold; Napoleon III had aluminium cutlery for top guests (silver for lesser). UPSC angle: metallurgy energy intensity vs sustainability — green hydrogen-based reduction (replacing carbon) being researched (e.g., Tata Steel's HYBRIT-style projects). PYQ FREQUENCY: extraction-method-by-reactivity in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.
